questions.question: Q1. Where does the heat in a motor winding come from?

answers.a: Friction between the propeller and the air
answers.b: Resistive loss in the copper, P = I^2 x R
answers.c: Heat conducted back from the battery
answers.d: Sunlight absorbed by the motor bell

explanations.a: Incorrect — aerodynamic drag loads the motor, but the heat that raises winding temperature is generated electrically inside the copper.
explanations.b: Correct — current through the winding resistance dissipates I^2 x R watts, and that is the dominant heat source.
explanations.c: Incorrect — the battery has its own losses, but it does not heat the motor.
explanations.d: Incorrect — irrelevant on a bench and negligible in flight.

questions.question: Q2. If the steady temperature rise above ambient is proportional to the square of current, what happens to the rise when you halve the current?

explanations.a: Incorrect — that would be true if the relationship were linear, but the loss goes as I^2.
explanations.b: Correct — halving I quarters I^2, so the heat and the steady rise both fall to a quarter. Backing a motor off slightly does far more for its temperature than it costs in thrust.
explanations.c: Incorrect — less current means less loss and a lower steady temperature.
explanations.d: Incorrect — this is the wrong direction entirely.

questions.question: Q3. The bench reports both a case temperature and a winding temperature. Which is higher, and why does the distinction matter?

answers.a: The case, because it is exposed to the air
answers.b: The winding, because heat is generated there and has to flow outward to reach the case, so a case sensor always under-reads the hotspot
answers.d: The winding, but only when the motor is switched off

explanations.a: Incorrect — being exposed to air makes the case cooler, not hotter.
explanations.b: Correct — heat flows from winding to case to air down a temperature gradient, so the winding is the hotspot. A sensor can only reach the case, which is why the reading always flatters the real condition.
explanations.c: Incorrect — they converge only when no heat is being generated.
explanations.d: Incorrect — the gradient exists whenever the motor is dissipating power, and vanishes once it is off.

questions.question: Q4. What does a thermal resistance R_th, in degrees Celsius per watt, tell you?

answers.a: How many watts a part can dissipate before failing
answers.b: How many degrees the part rises above ambient for each watt of heat it has to shed
answers.c: How fast the part heats up
answers.d: The electrical resistance of the part at temperature

explanations.a: Incorrect — that follows from R_th combined with a temperature limit, but is not what R_th states.
explanations.b: Correct — steady rise = P x R_th. A part with a high R_th is a poor heat path and runs hot for modest power.
explanations.c: Incorrect — the speed of heating is set by the time constant, which also involves thermal capacitance.
explanations.d: Incorrect — that is electrical resistance, a different quantity despite the similar name.

questions.question: Q5. Two motors are identical except that one is heavier. How does the extra mass affect its thermal behaviour?

answers.a: It reaches the same steady temperature but takes longer to get there
answers.b: It reaches a lower steady temperature instantly
answers.c: Mass has no thermal effect at all
answers.d: It heats up faster because there is more metal to warm

explanations.a: Correct — mass sets thermal capacitance C_th, which lengthens the time constant tau = R_th x C_th. More metal means more heat can be absorbed before the temperature moves, so it tolerates longer bursts.
explanations.b: Incorrect — the steady temperature is set by R_th and the power, not by mass.
explanations.c: Incorrect — mass directly determines how much heat the part stores per degree.
explanations.d: Incorrect — more thermal mass slows the temperature rise, it does not accelerate it.

questions.question: Q6. On a first-order heating curve, the thermal time constant tau is read at what point?

answers.a: Where the curve first becomes visible
answers.b: Where the temperature has risen 63.2% of the way from ambient to its final steady value
answers.c: Where the curve becomes completely flat
answers.d: At exactly half the final temperature

explanations.a: Incorrect — that depends on the resolution of the display, not on the physics.
explanations.b: Correct — after one time constant an exponential rise has completed 1 - 1/e, or about 63.2%, of its journey.
explanations.c: Incorrect — the curve approaches its final value asymptotically and never truly flattens.
explanations.d: Incorrect — 50% corresponds to about 0.69 tau, a different and less conventional marker.

questions.question: Q7. Winding insulation fails when it gets too hot. What is the practical consequence of a motor exceeding its insulation limit?

answers.a: The motor simply runs less efficiently until it cools
answers.b: The enamel breaks down, turns between windings short together, and the motor burns out
answers.c: The ESC automatically reduces power to protect it

explanations.a: Incorrect — insulation breakdown is permanent damage, not a temporary efficiency loss.
explanations.b: Correct — once the enamel melts, adjacent turns short, current rises further, and the failure is irreversible.
explanations.c: Incorrect — a basic ESC has no winding temperature sensor and cannot protect the motor this way.
explanations.d: Incorrect — propeller retention is a mechanical matter, unrelated to winding temperature.

questions.question: Q8. Copper resistance rises with temperature, at roughly 0.39% per degree Celsius. Why is this a concern rather than a curiosity?

answers.a: It makes the motor quieter as it warms
answers.b: It creates a feedback loop: hotter copper draws more current for the same voltage, which makes more heat, which raises resistance again
answers.c: It only affects the ESC, not the motor
answers.d: It causes the motor to spin faster as it warms

explanations.a: Incorrect — resistance has no bearing on acoustic output.
explanations.b: Correct — this is the thermal runaway loop. If cooling cannot keep pace with the growth in loss, temperature diverges instead of settling.
explanations.c: Incorrect — MOSFET resistance also rises with temperature, but the effect is present in both.
explanations.d: Incorrect — higher resistance reduces current and torque, which lowers RPM under load.

questions.question: Q9. Why does a spinning propeller help cool the motor beneath it?

answers.a: The propeller shades the motor from radiant heat
answers.b: Forced convection from the induced downwash removes heat far faster than still air, lowering the effective thermal resistance
answers.c: The propeller absorbs heat through the shaft and radiates it
answers.d: It does not; the propeller only adds load

explanations.a: Incorrect — radiation is a minor term here and shading is not the mechanism.
explanations.b: Correct — moving air raises the convective heat transfer coefficient, which lowers R_th, which lowers the steady temperature for the same dissipated power.
explanations.c: Incorrect — conduction through the shaft is a small path compared with convection from the bell.
explanations.d: Incorrect — the propeller does add load, but its wash is also a significant cooling mechanism.

questions.question: Q10. In the simulator, what is the ESC over-temperature limit?

explanations.a: Incorrect — 50 C is a comfortable operating temperature, not a limit.
explanations.b: Correct — the bench flags ESC over-temperature above 80 C, and the same 80 C ceiling is used as the motor's safe operating limit in the cooling module.
explanations.c: Incorrect — 150 C is in the region of motor winding insulation limits, well above what an ESC board tolerates.
explanations.d: Incorrect — this is far beyond any survivable board temperature.
